Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

In Florida, a home insured by Citizens Property Insurance with wind coverage must also carry flood insurance. In a high-risk zone (A or V) this has applied since 2023 (new policies from April 1, renewals from July 1), whatever the home is worth. Outside those zones it phases in by rebuilding cost: from January 1, 2026 at $400,000 or more, and from January 1, 2027 for all other Citizens homes. Condo-unit and no-wind policies are exempt.

Citizens does not sell flood insurance: the required flood policy comes from another insurer, the NFIP or a private one, and must at least match the NFIP's dwelling coverage or meet Florida's private flood insurance rules (s. 627.715).

At a closing: In Florida, a home seller must give the buyer a flood disclosure at or before the sales contract, saying whether the seller knows of flood damage during their ownership, filed a flood claim, or received flood aid (s. 689.302, F.S.).

78.1% of Broward County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 78.1% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 7.5% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood map: FEMA's current flood map for unincorporated Broward County took effect July 31, 2024. FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Broward County has 103 map panels, the oldest in effect since August 18, 2014 and the newest since July 31, 2024. FEMA has revised that map by 13 Letters of Map Revision, 9 of them in effect since January 1, 2021. FEMA's map service lists 8,557 rulings for owners here who asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone (Letters of Map Amendment): 6,536 took the building or some or all of the lot out, 1,103 found it already outside the zone as mapped, 656 were denied, 262 other or mixed. FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one. Rulings for owners who applied (not your home's odds; FEMA's map service gives no dates for them), counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here. FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Florida Department of Financial Services (consumer help).

Flooded? Work out the proof-of-loss deadline for an NFIP (National Flood Insurance Program) policy. If the President declares a major disaster or emergency for your area, FEMA's standard window to register for disaster aid is 60 days from that declaration date, and FEMA can extend it (44 CFR §206.112). A private (non-NFIP) flood policy sets its own claim deadlines; they are in that policy.

Buying now? Work out when a new NFIP policy, or added or increased NFIP coverage, starts. Without an exception, the earliest start is 12:01 a.m. local time on the 30th calendar day after the application date, if the insurer receives the form and full amount due within 10 calendar days of that date or they are mailed by certified mail within 4 calendar days; otherwise it is the 30th calendar day after the insurer receives them. With the map exception the same receipt rules apply, but the start is the next calendar day instead of the 30th. The map exception holds only if the insurer receives the form and full amount due within 13 months of the map revision's effective date; after that, the 30-day wait applies. With the loan exception, coverage starts at the time of the loan closing if the insurer receives the form and full amount due within 30 calendar days of closing when the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays, or within 10 calendar days when you or anyone else pays; otherwise the earliest start is the 30th calendar day after the insurer receives them. Contents-only coverage qualifies only if the contents are part of the security for the loan.





Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Broward County, Florida: what floods pay out

Floods in Broward County have led to 33,026 NFIP flood claims and $456.3 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2023, 2024 and 2017.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2023 ($248,939,200), 2024 ($35,107,673), 2017 ($24,329,084). Total paid $456,267,154. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: of the 7,949 claims here with a flood zone on the claim, losses 2016–2025, 18.7% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D), and they got 7.4% of the dollars paid on those claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 32.6% of the 42,859 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 42,859 policies reporting one)32.6%Florida: 38.5%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)86.4%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 16,417 claims paid with a damage figure)0.5%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $792 a year (Zone AHB) to $854 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? The premium is based on the flood risk of the building. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How much flood risk is here?

Very High for coastal flooding and Very High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $14.1 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: coastal flood loss here is higher than in about 71% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $289.0 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 66% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 13, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $166.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $535 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 13, 2026.
